facts.text: Fun detail: the 20th Century Fox logo at the start plays without its famous fanfare, so the movie opens in eerie quiet.
Frank (Warren Oates) calls a mechanic 'L.Q.' Oates really worked with actor L.Q. Jones on three Sam Peckinpah films.
Peter Fonda and Warren Oates reportedly signed on partly because Oates' 15-year-old daughter read the script and approved of it.
That gleaming 32-foot motorhome is a 1975 Vogue Villa Grande. In the script it carried a $36,000 price tag, a huge sum in 1975.
Loretta Swit (Alice) really drove the RV through downtown San Antonio herself while Peter Fonda and Warren Oates yelled 'Brake, Loretta, brake!'
Frank brags the RV has a 'stereo, four channels.' A plain stereo only has two; four-channel would be quadraphonic. Salesman-speak!
Lara Parker (Kelly) was famous as witch Angelique on the gothic soap Dark Shadows. She later wrote four novels about that character.
The characters' January ski trip matched reality: principal photography began in January 1975 in Texas. Yet everyone swims in the RV park pool later on.
It was shot in Bandera, San Antonio, Castroville, Tarpley and Leakey, Texas. Loretta Swit called it a 'touring shoot' where 'we kept moving.'
Peter Fonda reportedly did most of his own stunts and insisted the movie include dirt bike racing, like this motorcycle race between his and Warren Oates' characters.
This was the second of three films pairing Peter Fonda and Warren Oates, after The Hired Hand (1971) and before 92 in the Shade (1975).
Peter Fonda: most of the shoot was at night. Fonda and Warren Oates taped 'do not disturb before 4:30 p.m.' signs to their doors, in Spanish and English.
Director Jack Starrett claimed he hired real Satanists as hooded cult extras. Wikipedia says that was likely a publicity stunt.
Asked years later if director Jack Starrett hired real Satanists as extras, Loretta Swit denied it, joking there were no little Satanists in Texas.
Writer Lee Frost was hired to direct but was replaced by Jack Starrett a week into shooting. Fox executives learned most of the dialogue was being improvised.
After director Lee Frost was fired, stars Peter Fonda and Warren Oates reportedly barricaded themselves in their hotel room. Oates later flipped a glass coffee table at a tense meeting.
Warren Oates starred in Sam Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch (1969). He turned down the lead in Support Your Local Sheriff! to make it.
Sheriff Taylor is played by R.G. Armstrong, a Sam Peckinpah regular (Ride the High Country, Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid) who was best friends with Andy Griffith.
Director Jack Starrett was Gabby Johnson in Blazing Saddles (1974) and the brutal deputy in First Blood (1982). Mel Brooks cast him after seeing his drunk routine at a party.
Peter Fonda's boasts about accidentally shooting himself as a kid reportedly inspired John Lennon's Beatles song 'She Said She Said.'
The library book's human sacrifice picture comes from H.M. Herget's Aztec life paintings in the June 1937 National Geographic.
Lara Parker said on the DVD commentary that she had been dating director Jack Starrett. She and Peter Fonda's sister Jane Fonda were also Vassar roommates.
The film's working title was 'So Mote It Be', the phrase on the threatening rune left on the RV's broken window.
Loretta Swit (Alice) was M*A*S*H's Hot Lips Houlihan, and she never saw the movie M*A*S*H before being offered that role. This was her only horror film.
Continuity slip: the group vacations in January and wears heavy coats, yet everyone is swimming at the RV park pool.
AFI's catalog says the production employed over 100 Texas actors and crew, with Paul Knuckles as stunt coordinator.
Clay Tanner plays the motor lodge Satanist here. In Rosemary's Baby (1968) he played the Devil himself.
The dog hanging from the RV door was a real dog, drugged beforehand, and completely unharmed.
During the rattlesnake scenes, the snakes kept striking and one reportedly urinated all over Peter Fonda's shirt when he picked it up.
The rattlers weren't defanged. Loretta Swit said venom was milked on set, and she watched it happen. She came to think of the snakes as fellow actors.
UK censors required cuts to the snake being struck with a pole, under animal cruelty rules, before giving it a 15 certificate.
Body count: 9 humans, 2 dogs and 2 rattlesnakes.
Frank says the oil cooler is 'mashed up against the radiator,' but the RV's grill shows no damage.
The shotgun Frank and Roger buy is a Remington 870 pump, a gun still popular today.
Plot hole: Frank walks out with a shotgun and two boxes of buckshot without filling out any paperwork.
Gas station attendant: director Jack Starrett himself, in a cameo. He called Race with the Devil his favorite of his own movies.
Stunt count: sixteen cars, two trucks and eight motorcycles were destroyed, per an August 1975 Los Angeles Times report cited by AFI.
The RV chase footage, with the motorhome getting more battered, was reused as stock footage in an episode of the TV series The Fall Guy (1981).
Richard Scheib of Moria likened the film to the Mad Max 2 tanker chase stretched to feature length, with hooded Satanists as raiders. He noted the Devil never appears.
It was a hit: over $12 million domestic gross for 20th Century Fox, about $5.8 million in North American rentals, and a drive-in staple for years.
The New York Times panned it as 'a ridiculous mishmash of a movie for people who never grew up.' Variety's Joseph McBride praised the performances, Leonard Rosenman's score and the action.
Time Out praised it as 'a winner all the way,' a surprise since Jack Starrett's directing record was 'the movie director's equivalent of a criminal record.'
Kevin Smith says this film strongly influenced his 2011 thriller Red State. It also inspired Nicolas Cage's Drive Angry (2011) and the Tamil film Kazhugu (1981).
The 2017 horror comedy Party Bus to Hell names its characters after this film's characters and actors as a homage.
A remake was announced in 2005, to be directed by Chris Moore of Project Greenlight and written by Drew McWeeny and Scott Swan. It never appeared.
